The three temples

Instead of a single Capitol, Sufetula built three separate temples side by side in the 2nd century, for Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, linked by arches. They are among the best-preserved Roman temples in North Africa.
The Antonine gate

The monumental entrance to the forum, a gate of three arches dedicated in 139 CE to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons. Through it, the three temples appear framed at the end of the square.
Arch of the Tetrarchy
A triumphal arch of about 300 CE, at the southern entrance of the town, dedicated to the four emperors who then shared the empire, Diocletian and Maximian with their deputies.
Built on the bank of the wadi, with the river behind the stage. Some columns of the stage front have been raised again; the theatre hosts the Sbeitla spring festival.
Church of Vitalis
A large Christian basilica of the 5th–6th century with five aisles. Its baptistery keeps a baptismal font lined with bright mosaics of crosses, fish and candles.
Church of Bellator
One of the great churches of the town centre, named after Bellator, who appears in an inscription. Its columns still mark the nave and aisles; beside it stands the small chapel of Bishop Jucundus.
The great baths
Public baths with cold, warm and hot rooms, a palaestra for exercise, and floors on small brick pillars so that hot air from the furnaces could run underneath.
The Byzantine forts

In the 6th and 7th centuries, the Byzantines turned houses and buildings of the old town into small forts. In 647 the first Arab army defeated the exarch Gregory near Sufetula, the start of the Muslim conquest of Ifriqiya.

The Ghriba synagogue

By tradition the oldest synagogue in Africa, founded by priests who fled Jerusalem after the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE. The present building dates mostly from the late 19th century. Every spring, for Lag BaOmer, pilgrims come from Tunisia and abroad.
Inside the Ghriba

Walls of blue tiles, white arches on blue columns, a painted wooden ceiling and brass lamps. Visitors take off their shoes and cover their heads; the Torah scrolls are kept in the Ark at the end of the hall.
The pilgrims’ caravanserai
Beside the synagogue, a large guesthouse with two storeys of rooms round a courtyard, built to lodge the pilgrims who come for the annual festival.
Djerbahood

In 2014 about 150 street artists from some 30 countries painted the walls of Erriadh, turning the old village of Hara Sghira into an open-air gallery. The murals here are generated, in the spirit of the real ones.
The mosques of Djerba
The island has hundreds of small mosques, many of the Ibadi tradition: white, thick-walled and sometimes fortified, with short minarets, once used as lookouts against raiders from the sea.
A menzel among the palms

Instead of large villages, Djerbians long lived in scattered family estates: white houses with vaulted and domed rooms round a courtyard, a cistern for rainwater, and palms and olive trees around. This way of settling the island is why Djerba was listed by UNESCO in 2023.
A country shrine
Small white domed shrines such as Sidi Salama El Jenaouni stand among the fields, tombs of holy men visited by the people of the island.

Hotel Sidi Driss

A family house of several courtyard pits joined by underground passages, now a hotel. In 1976 this courtyard was filmed as the home of Luke Skywalker in Star Wars, which made Matmata known around the world.
A room in the rock

Vaulted rooms are dug into the soft rock all round the courtyard and lime-washed inside. Under several metres of earth they stay cool in the summer heat and mild on winter nights. The upper openings are granaries for grain and oil.
The entrance tunnel

The only way in is a sloping tunnel, the sqifa, dug from the hillside down to the courtyard. A sunken lane leads to its whitewashed mouth; inside, it was also a place to keep animals and to receive visitors.
Dar Khadija

A troglodyte house kept as a small museum, furnished as a Berber family lived in it, with the tools of daily life in the rooms round the courtyard. Several families often shared one house, each with its own rooms.
An abandoned courtyard

In 1969 weeks of rain soaked the soft rock and many pits collapsed. Many families moved to New Matmata, built on the plain to the north, and many courtyards have stood empty since. (This pit is generated, among the mapped ones.)
A village of craters

Seen from the hills, Matmata is a field of round holes. Its Berber people dug their houses into the soft rock of the Dahar hills, sheltered from the heat and wind, with olive trees and palms in the hollows where the rain water gathers behind small earth dams (jessour).
The village above ground
The mosque, the shops and the newer stone houses of Matmata stand above ground, on the hill around which the pits are dug. Some families still live in their courtyards; others open them to visitors.

The second courtyard

In the 19th century the ksar was extended with a second courtyard, bringing it to around 400 ghorfas. The tribes of the plain kept their harvests here, safe from raids, and came back to fetch grain and oil as they needed them.
The first courtyard

The oldest part of the ksar, often dated to the 15th century (some historians say 1699): vaulted ghorfas stacked four storeys high around a closed courtyard. In 1997 it was filmed for Star Wars: The Phantom Menace.
Inside a ghorfa

Each ghorfa is a long barrel-vaulted cell of stone and mud plaster, with a small wooden door. Thick walls kept grain, oil and dried food cool and dry through the summer; each family had its own cells.
Stairs without railings
Narrow stair ramps of plastered stone climb the walls to the upper doors. Beam ends sticking out under the doors served as footholds and to hoist sacks up by rope.
Between the two courtyards
A short passage, roofed with palm trunks, joins the two courtyards.
On the hilltop
From outside the ksar shows almost blank walls: a fortress of granaries on a hilltop of the Dahar, about 20 km south of Tataouine, above the village that took its name.
